title: Background jobs with a queue
summary: The API drops slow work onto SQS and returns at once; a pool of Fargate workers drains the queue at a steady pace.
intro: Some work is too slow to do while a user waits: resizing a video, generating a PDF, calling a flaky partner API. The API puts a message describing the job on a queue and responds right away. Workers pull jobs when they have capacity, so a sudden burst piles up in the queue instead of overwhelming anything, and a crashed worker’s job simply becomes visible again for another worker.
fits: Any app with slow or bursty side work

diagram.caption: Uploads arrive in bursts. The API enqueues a job for each and moves on. The queue only hands a job to a worker that has room, so the backlog grows during a burst and drains steadily after it. Results land in S3.

steps.title: The API enqueues and returns
steps.text: For each upload, the API sends a small message such as `{"job": "thumbnail", "key": "uploads/123.jpg"}` to SQS and replies `202 Accepted`. The user isn’t kept waiting for the processing.

steps.title: Workers pull when they’re free
steps.text: Each worker long-polls the queue, takes a job, and the message becomes invisible to others for the visibility timeout. During a burst the queue absorbs the excess instead of the workers.

steps.title: Success deletes the message
steps.text: When the thumbnail is written to S3, the worker deletes the message. If the worker crashes first, the message reappears after the timeout and another worker retries it.

steps.title: Scale on queue depth
steps.text: An autoscaling rule watches how many messages are waiting and adds workers when the backlog grows, then removes them when it’s empty.

good: Users get fast responses regardless of how slow the job is
Bursts are smoothed out: workers run at a steady rate instead of falling over
Retries come for free, and a dead-letter queue catches jobs that keep failing
API and workers scale and deploy independently
watch: Standard SQS queues can deliver a message more than once; make jobs idempotent
Set the visibility timeout longer than your slowest job, or jobs run twice
Users need a way to learn the job finished: polling, a webhook or a notification
A growing backlog is a silent failure; alert on the age of the oldest message

swaps.text: Short jobs (under 15 minutes)? Let Lambda consume the queue directly and skip managing workers.
Self-hosted, or need routing and priorities? RabbitMQ is the classic open-source broker for this.
Already on Postgres? pgmq or PgQueuer keep jobs in the same database, so a job can be enqueued in the same transaction as the data it’s about.
Multi-step jobs with retries per step and long waits fit a workflow engine better than a bare queue.
